intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that otofaciocervical syndrome-1 (OTFCS1) is caused by mutation in the EYA1 gene on chromosome 8q13.3, either as part of a de novo contiguous deletion of EYA1 and the surrounding region or as a point mutation within EYA1.

checks.claim: Otofaciocervical syndrome-1 (OTFCS1) is caused by mutation in the EYA1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: One patient with OFC syndrome carried a large deletion of the EYA1 gene region, confirming that OFC syndrome is allelic with BOR syndrome.
checks.explanation: The paper reports a deletion that includes EYA1, which counts as a mutation in the broad sense. The point-mutation route mentioned in the paragraph is not in this paper.

checks.claim: The EYA1 gene is located on chromosome 8q13.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations in the EYA1 gene (localised to 8q13.3)
checks.explanation: The abstract states this location directly.

checks.claim: OTFCS1 can be caused by a de novo contiguous deletion of EYA1 and the surrounding region.
checks.evidence_quote: has identified de novo deletions of the EYA1 gene and surrounding region in two patients with complex phenotypes involving features of BOR syndrome. One patient with OFC syndrome carried a large deletion of the EYA1 gene region
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a de novo deletion of EYA1 and the surrounding region, and the title calls OFC a contiguous gene deletion syndrome.

checks.claim: OTFCS1 can be caused by a point mutation within EYA1.
checks.evidence_quote: we show here that an OFC patient bears a single-nucleotide substitution in a splice site of EYA1.
checks.explanation: The abstract describes a point mutation in EYA1 in an OFC patient.

paragraphs.text: Otofaciocervical syndrome is a developmental disorder that resembles branchiootorenal (BOR) syndrome. Rickard et al. (2001) described it as clinically similar to BOR syndrome but having features in addition to those of BOR syndrome. Estefanía et al. (2006) characterized it by trophic alterations of the facies and shoulder girdle in addition to the malformations seen in BOR.

checks.claim: Otofaciocervical syndrome is a developmental disorder that resembles branchiootorenal (BOR) syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The distinction between BOR and other dysplasias, such as oto-facio-cervical syndrome (OFC), is challenged by frequent association of the former to other diverse malformations
checks.explanation: The abstract calls OFC a dysplasia that is hard to tell apart from BOR, so it resembles BOR.

checks.claim: Rickard et al. (2001) described otofaciocervical syndrome as clinically similar to BOR syndrome but having features in addition to those of BOR syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Oto-facio-cervical (OFC) syndrome is clinically similar to BOR syndrome, with clinical features in addition to those of BOR syndrome.
checks.explanation: The claim restates this sentence of the abstract.

checks.claim: Estefanía et al. (2006) characterized otofaciocervical syndrome by trophic alterations of the facies and shoulder girdle in addition to the malformations seen in BOR syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: OFC is characterized by trophic alterations of the facies and shoulder girdle in addition to the malformations seen in BOR.
checks.explanation: This is stated directly.

paragraphs.text: Fára et al. (1967) reported familial otofaciocervical dysmorphia. Dallapiccola and Mingarelli (1995) noted that some features present in the original family, including lateral cervical fistulae, had suggested that OFC syndrome could be a variant of BOR syndrome.

checks.evidence_quote: [Familial oto-facio-cervical dysmorphia].
checks.explanation: The title says the paper reports familial otofaciocervical dysmorphia.

checks.claim: Dallapiccola and Mingarelli (1995) noted that some features present in the original OFC syndrome family, including lateral cervical fistulae, had suggested that OFC syndrome could be a variant of BOR syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: Some features present in the original family, including lateral cervical fistulae, have suggested that OFC syndrome could be a variant of BOR syndrome.
checks.explanation: Stated directly in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Dallapiccola and Mingarelli (1995) described a sporadic patient with OFC syndrome. Distinguishing features were a long face with narrow nose, high arched palate, prominent and dysmorphic ears, long neck, sloping shoulders and clavicles, winged, low, and laterally set scapulae, tetralogy of Fallot, and deafness secondary to cochlear malformation. Preauricular tags, lacrimal duct stenosis, and renal malformations were absent. The authors concluded that the absence of these features, together with the distinct facial and radiographic findings and markedly downward sloping shoulders, supported OFC syndrome being a unique, clinically recognizable entity distinct from BOR syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Pohl et al. (2013) found a homozygous mutation in the PAX1 gene (c.497G-T, gly166-to-val (G166V)) that cosegregated with disease in a large consanguineous Turkish family with autosomal recessive otofaciocervical syndrome, characterized by facial dysmorphism, external ear anomalies with preauricular pits and hearing impairment, branchial cysts or fistulas, anomalies of the vertebrae and shoulder girdle, and mild intellectual disability. The variant was found by whole-exome sequencing of a pooled DNA sample from 4 affected individuals. In a dual luciferase reporter assay, the corresponding mouse mutant Pax1(G157V) showed significantly reduced transactivation of a regulatory sequence in the Nkx3-2 promoter compared with wildtype.

checks.evidence_quote: In a large consanguineous family with OFCS from Turkey, we performed whole-exome sequencing (WES)
checks.explanation: The abstract states the family was large, consanguineous and from Turkey, and that OFCS is autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: Pohl et al. (2013) found a homozygous c.497G-T (G166V) mutation in the PAX1 gene in the affected members of a large consanguineous Turkish family with otofaciocervical syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: identified only a single novel homozygous variant, c.497G>T, located in PAX1 that co-segregated with the disease in the family.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports a homozygous c.497G>T variant in PAX1, predicted as p.G166V.

checks.explanation: The abstract states the variant cosegregated with the disease.

paragraphs.text: Using a fluorescent quantitative multiplex PCR dosage assay for 3 3-prime exons (7, 9, and 13) of the EYA1 gene, combined with microsatellite marker analysis, Rickard et al. (2001) identified de novo deletions of the EYA1 gene and surrounding region in 2 patients with complex phenotypes involving features of BOR syndrome. One patient with OFC syndrome carried a large deletion of the EYA1 gene region, which the authors interpreted as confirming that OFC syndrome is allelic with BOR syndrome and is a contiguous gene deletion syndrome involving EYA1. Comparison of the boundaries of this deletion with other reported rearrangements of the region reduced the critical region for Duane syndrome to between markers D8S553 and D8S1797, a genetic distance of approximately 1 cM.

checks.evidence_quote: We have developed a fluorescent quantitative multiplex polymerase chain reaction for three 3' exons (7, 9 and 13) of the EYA1 gene. This dosage assay, combined with microsatellite marker analysis
checks.explanation: The method matches the abstract, including the three exons.

checks.explanation: The abstract states this directly.

checks.explanation: The genetic distance matches the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Estefanía et al. (2006) identified a single-nucleotide substitution in a splice site of the EYA1 gene in a patient with OFC syndrome. The authors concluded that not only major rearrangements, but also point mutations altering the EYA1 reading frame, can be found in patients with OFC syndrome, in contrast to the hypothesis that OFC is caused by contiguous deletions of EYA1 and adjacent genes.

checks.claim: Estefanía et al. (2006) presented their finding of an EYA1 point mutation in OFC syndrome as contrasting with the hypothesis that OFC syndrome is caused by contiguous deletions of EYA1 and adjacent genes.

checks.explanation: The authors explicitly present their finding as contrasting with the contiguous-deletion hypothesis.

agent.process_note: All 5 files were read in full: 4 abstracts and 1 title only (Fára et al., 1967). EYA1 was taken as the causal gene based on Rickard et al. (2001), who found a de novo large deletion, and Estefanía et al. (2006), who found a splice-site point mutation. Neither abstract gives the exact nucleotide change, exon or deletion size, or explicitly states zygosity, so no allelic variants were listed and the intro does not state a zygosity. The AD inheritance recorded for EYA1 is an inference from the de novo deletion, not an explicit statement in the papers. PAX1 (Pohl et al., 2013) concerns autosomal recessive OFCS, which is treated as a separate type, so it is described under Heterogeneity only. No gene MIM numbers were supplied, so none were written.
